workflow_configuration.task_objective: Build a B2B SaaS business by treating product-market fit as an empirical state to be measured, not a milestone to be declared: a specific, reachable segment with an urgent, expensive problem; a product that segment adopts, retains, and expands on; and an acquisition motion whose unit economics improve with scale. The architectural approach is sequential and gated — nail the problem before the product, the product before the channel, the channel before the spend — because capital deployed upstream of validation converts errors into liabilities. Sustainable, low-churn growth is defined quantitatively: net revenue retention above 100% (the business grows even with zero new logos), gross logo churn trending under ~1–2% monthly for SMB and materially lower for mid-market/enterprise, LTV:CAC at or above 3:1 with CAC payback under 12–18 months, and at least one acquisition loop whose output compounds (each cohort of customers or content makes the next cohort cheaper to acquire) rather than a set of paid channels that reset to zero each month. Retention is the foundation: acquisition poured into a leaking product is capital destruction, so churn is diagnosed and fixed before acquisition is scaled. Every strategic claim in this workflow must be falsifiable — stated as a metric with a threshold and a time window — and every phase ends with a kill/pivot/proceed decision made against pre-committed criteria, not against sunk cost or enthusiasm.
workflow_configuration.market_analysis: 1. Define the ideal customer profile (ICP) from evidence, not aspiration: start from the customers (or design partners) who adopted fastest, pay the most relative to cost-to-serve, churn least, and refer others; extract their shared observable traits — firmographics (industry, headcount, revenue band, tooling stack, regulatory environment), the triggering event that made the problem urgent (funding round, compliance deadline, scaling break-point, incumbent price hike), and the buying structure (who feels the pain, who evaluates, who signs, who can veto). An ICP that cannot be turned into a filterable prospect list is a persona, not a profile. 2. Quantify the pain in the customer's currency: for the candidate problem, establish what it costs the buyer today — hours, headcount, error rates, lost revenue, audit risk — through 15–25 problem-discovery interviews per segment that ask about current behavior and past spending, never about hypothetical intent ("what do you do today, what have you tried, what did it cost" — not "would you use this"). Evidence of budget already being spent on workarounds (spreadsheets plus a contractor, a misused adjacent tool, an internal script someone maintains) is the strongest signal; a pain nobody has tried to solve is usually a pain nobody will pay to solve. 3. Segment and rank the market by beachhead quality, not TAM: score candidate segments on urgency of pain, ability to pay, accessibility (can you reach 100 of them repeatably through one channel), competitive vacancy, and word-of-mouth density (do buyers in this segment talk to each other — communities, associations, conferences). Choose one beachhead deliberately narrow enough to dominate; a startup that averages two segments loses both. Size it bottom-up (number of ICP-matching accounts × realistic ACV × plausible penetration), and treat top-down TAM slides as marketing, not analysis. 4. Map the real competitive set from the buyer's chair: the competition is whatever the buyer would do instead — named vendors, the incumbent suite that "already has a module for that", internal builds, spreadsheets, and doing nothing. For each, document what the buyer gains and loses by choosing it, actual pricing as negotiated (not list), contract structure and switching costs, and the sales motion it uses. "Do nothing" is usually the largest competitor; its vulnerability is the cost-of-inaction quantified in step 2. 5. Analyze competitor vulnerabilities systematically, from primary sources: mine competitors' public review streams (G2, Capterra, app marketplaces, Reddit, community forums) for recurring complaint clusters — pricing model resentment, mandatory implementation fees, support decay post-acquisition, missing integrations, performance at scale, contract lock-in anger; read their release notes and job postings to infer roadmap direction and organizational strain; interview their churned customers (they are findable and willing) for the real reason they left versus the stated one. Classify each vulnerability as structural (rooted in their business model, pricing architecture, or install base — they cannot fix it without harming themselves) versus incidental (a missing feature they can ship next quarter). Position only against structural vulnerabilities; incidental gaps are a roadmap race you lose to the better-funded player. 6. Identify the wedge and the moat hypothesis: the wedge is the narrowest capability that lands you inside the account despite the incumbent (a 10x improvement on one workflow, an integration the incumbent refuses to build, a pricing model the incumbent's margins forbid); the moat hypothesis is what compounds after landing — workflow embedment, accumulated data, network effects across accounts, or switching costs you earn honestly. Write both down with the evidence for each; a wedge without a moat hypothesis is a feature waiting to be absorbed. 7. Exit criterion: a one-page ICP with a buildable prospect list of at least 100 matching accounts, quantified pain with source interviews, one chosen beachhead with bottom-up sizing, a competitor vulnerability map distinguishing structural from incidental weaknesses, and a written wedge-and-moat hypothesis — each element falsifiable and dated.

growth_execution.phase_1_positioning: 1. Anchor positioning in the alternative, not the category: state what the buyer uses today, what that costs them (from market_analysis step 2), and what specifically changes when they switch. The value proposition formula: for [ICP] who [triggering situation], [product] eliminates [named pain] unlike [the real alternative], which [structural vulnerability] — every clause filled with researched fact, none with adjectives. 2. Translate every capability into outcome language at three altitudes: the user's workflow ("close the books in 3 days instead of 12"), the buyer's business case ("reclaim 1.5 FTE in the finance team"), and the executive's strategic frame ("audit-ready continuously, not quarterly"). Feature lists appear only after the pain-outcome pairing is established, and only as evidence for the claimed outcome. If a feature cannot be attached to a named pain from the interview corpus, it does not appear on the landing page. 3. Make the claim specific, quantified, and falsifiable: "reduce reconciliation time 80%" with a customer-verifiable mechanism beats "streamline your workflow" in every test. Use the customers' own vocabulary harvested from interviews and reviews — the words they used to describe the pain are the words that make them feel understood; internal jargon and invented category names repel the very buyers who have the problem. 4. Choose the positioning axis competitors cannot follow: position on the structural vulnerability identified in market_analysis (their pricing architecture, their neglected segment, their forced platform migration), so that every competitor response reinforces your frame. Positioning on an incidental gap invites a feature-parity announcement that erases the message. 5. Test positioning empirically before scaling it: run the message in cold outbound subject lines and landing-page variants against the prospect list; measure reply rate, demo-request rate, and — most diagnostic — whether prospects repeat the positioning back in their own words on discovery calls. Sales-call recordings are the assay: when prospects begin describing the problem using your framing, positioning has landed; when every call requires re-explaining the category, it has not. 6. Propagate one message architecture everywhere: the same pain-outcome-proof structure in the deck, the website, onboarding, and pricing page, versioned in a single source-of-truth document. Positioning drift across surfaces reintroduces the confusion positioning exists to remove. 7. Exit criterion: a written positioning document (ICP, trigger, pain, outcome, alternative, structural differentiation, proof), cold-channel evidence that the message converts strangers to conversations at a repeatable rate, and call recordings demonstrating buyers echo the framing unprompted.
growth_execution.phase_2_acquisition_loops: 1. Distinguish loops from channels before allocating anything: a channel is a faucet (paid ads, cold outbound) whose output stops when effort stops and whose cost typically rises with scale; a loop is a system whose output feeds its own input (content that ranks compounds authority which ranks new content faster; users who invite users; customers whose public artifacts recruit their peers). Build the business on one or two loops; use faucets to prime loops and to smooth demand, never as the terminal growth architecture. 2. Earn the right to scale with a manual, unscalable motion first: founder-led outbound and founder-led sales against the beachhead list until the pitch, objections, close rate, and onboarding are understood firsthand — typically through the first 10–20 paying customers. This motion does not scale and is not supposed to; it produces the conversion benchmarks, objection map, and champion profiles that every subsequent loop is calibrated against. 3. Select loop candidates by ICP behavior, not by fashion: where does the ICP already look when the triggering event fires — search queries with commercial intent (SEO/content loop), peers and communities (referral and community loops), an existing platform's marketplace (integration/ecosystem loop), or artifacts shared across company boundaries (collaborative virality)? B2B SaaS defaults worth testing: pain-point SEO plus comparison content; a free tool or calculator that solves a sliver of the problem and captures intent; integration marketplaces of the systems the ICP already lives in; customer-visible outputs (reports, portals, shared workspaces) that expose the product to non-users; structured referral/affiliate programs priced against measured LTV. 4. Architect each loop explicitly before funding it: write the loop diagram — input (new user/content/customer), action, output, and how output re-enters as input — plus the loop's cycle time and its quantitative multiplier (e.g., invites sent per active account × acceptance rate; articles published per month × ranking rate × visitor-to-signup rate). A loop whose multiplier is below self-sustainment can still be worth running (it discounts blended CAC) but must be labeled as an assisted loop, not a compounding one. 5. Test loops sequentially with kill criteria, not in parallel with hope: one loop at a time gets a bounded budget and a pre-committed success threshold (from decision_gates); instrument the full funnel (first-touch through activation through revenue, with honest attribution) before the first dollar; run to statistical adequacy; then kill, iterate, or scale. Three loops tested at 30% intensity produce three ambiguous readings; one loop tested properly produces a decision. 6. Match the motion to the economics: ACV bounds the acquisition architecture — sub-$5k ACV cannot support human-touch sales and must convert through self-serve, product-led onboarding, and low-touch loops; $25k+ ACV supports SDR/AE motion where loops feed pipeline rather than direct signup; the dead zone in between kills more SaaS companies than competition does — resolve it by moving price up (packaging, tier design) or touch down (PLG), not by wishing the math away. 7. Reinvest in the loop's compounding asset: for content loops, topical authority and internal linking; for ecosystem loops, marketplace ranking and co-marketing; for referral loops, the moments of peak realized value (post-outcome, not post-signup) where the ask converts best. The loop's asset should appear on the balance sheet of the strategy even though accounting ignores it: it is the reason next year's CAC is lower than this year's. 8. Exit criterion: one loop demonstrably compounding or two assisted loops with stable-or-declining blended CAC, full-funnel instrumentation with cohort attribution, unit economics passing the decision_gates thresholds at current scale, and a written model of each loop's multiplier with actuals against forecast.
growth_execution.phase_3_retention: 1. Instrument retention as cohort curves, not averages: monthly logo retention and net revenue retention by acquisition cohort, segmented by ICP-fit, plan, channel, and onboarding path. The single most important shape: does the cohort curve flatten to a stable asymptote (a retained core exists — a product some segment cannot live without) or decline linearly to zero (no PMF for that segment, and acquisition into it is destroying capital)? Blended averages conceal exactly this distinction. 2. Define and validate the activation event: the earliest in-product behavior that statistically separates long-retained accounts from churned ones (the workflow completed, the integration connected, the second user invited, the first report shared). Validate the correlation on historical cohorts, then point the entire onboarding at that event and manage time-to-activation as a first-class metric; most churn is decided in the first weeks and merely recorded months later. 3. Track the leading indicators, review them weekly: activation rate and time-to-activation; breadth and depth of usage (seats active / seats sold, core actions per account per week); NRR and gross churn by cohort; expansion rate; support ticket sentiment and time-to-resolution; champion departure (the single highest-signal enterprise churn predictor — instrument job-change detection for named champions); renewal-risk composite for accounts under contract. Lagging indicators (the churn number itself) are for measurement; leading indicators are for action. 4. Run the qualitative loops on a fixed cadence, with the findings routed to owners: (a) churn autopsies — a structured exit interview or call for every churned account above threshold ACV, coded into a stable taxonomy (bad-fit acquisition, unrealized value, missing capability, champion left, price/value mismatch, consolidation/M&A), reviewed monthly with one named action per top cluster; (b) activation-failure interviews — accounts that signed but never activated, the richest vein of onboarding defects; (c) win/loss and renewal interviews for the counterfactual view; (d) in-product micro-surveys (NPS/CSAT/effort) used as conversation triggers, not as vanity dashboards. Qualitative findings must land in the same prioritization forum as the roadmap, or they decorate rather than steer. 5. Attack churn by root cause class, in order of leverage: (1) bad-fit acquisition — churned accounts that never matched the ICP are an acquisition defect, fixed by tightening targeting and disqualification, not by product work; (2) activation failure — fixed by onboarding redesign toward the validated activation event, success-team intervention on stalled accounts, and removing time-to-value obstacles; (3) unrealized ongoing value — fixed by usage-triggered playbooks, QBR/value-review motions that restate delivered outcomes in the buyer's currency, and product work on the retained core's actual workflow; (4) structural exposure — single-champion dependency (fix: multi-thread every account above threshold ACV), missing integrations that make the product peripheral (fix: embed in the system of record), and contract design (annual prepaid with implementation removes the monthly exit ramp for segments that tolerate it honestly). 6. Route retention data back into the growth engine: churn-reason clusters re-rank the roadmap; bad-fit patterns re-tighten the ICP and the acquisition targeting; activation insights reshape onboarding and positioning promises (churn born of overpromise is a positioning defect, fixed in phase 1, not a success-team failure); NRR by channel re-prices what each acquisition loop is actually worth. Retention is not a department downstream of growth; it is the measurement system that tells the growth engine the truth. 7. Exit criterion (continuous, reviewed monthly): cohort curves flattening for the core ICP; NRR ≥ 100% (≥ 110% where expansion tiers exist); gross churn within the segment-appropriate band; churn-reason taxonomy current with every top cluster owned; activation event validated and trending; and a demonstrated case each quarter of retention data changing an acquisition or roadmap decision.

critical_pitfalls.pitfall: Hiring sales teams, buying traffic, and building infrastructure before retention proves the bucket holds — the most documented startup killer. Scaling multiplies whatever exists: scaled PMF compounds, scaled churn incinerates capital. Prevention: the decision_gates below are hard-blocking; acquisition spend is capped until cohort curves flatten and payback is measured, not projected.

Shipping whatever the loudest prospect or largest deal demands, until the product is a thin layer over every workflow and a deep solution to none — positioning dies first, then velocity, then retention. Prevention: every feature request maps to the ICP's ranked pain list or is declined; one-customer features are custom work priced accordingly or refused; the roadmap forum weighs churn-autopsy clusters above deal-desk pressure.

Growing on blended, unexamined CAC/LTV — counting logos while payback stretches past 24 months and LTV rests on retention assumptions no cohort has demonstrated. Prevention: LTV computed only from observed cohort retention (never from target churn); CAC fully loaded (salaries, tools, agency fees — not just ad spend); reviewed per channel and per segment monthly, because blended numbers hide the channel that is quietly unprofitable.

Steering by signups, page views, cumulative users, and MRR-with-churn-netted-out, all of which rise while the business dies. Prevention: the operating dashboard leads with cohort retention, NRR, activation rate, CAC payback, and burn multiple; any metric that cannot fall is banned from decision contexts.

Mistaking enthusiasm for fit — pilots that never convert, design partners who use it free but will not pay, friends-and-family logos, one whale whose spend masks universal churn beneath. Prevention: PMF evidence is defined as strangers paying full price and retaining; concentration above ~20% of revenue in one account triggers a diversification flag; pilot-to-paid conversion is tracked as its own metric.

One channel driving >70% of acquisition — an algorithm update, policy change, or CPC inflation away from a growth stop; worse when the channel is rented (a marketplace or platform that can change terms). Prevention: concentration monitored quarterly; the loop portfolio always contains one owned asset (content authority, community, email list) whose economics the platform cannot repossess.

Pricing at a point that can support neither self-serve volume nor a sales team — too expensive for a credit card, too cheap for an AE. Prevention: packaging designed against the motion (PLG tier below, sales-assisted tier above); ACV × close rate × volume checked against the cost of the motion before hiring for it.

Founder-led sales works, then the founder becomes the permanent, unscalable channel because nothing was documented. Prevention: the founder-sales phase produces artifacts by mandate — recorded calls, objection playbook, qualification criteria, pricing floors — and the first sales hires are measured against that documented baseline, not against the founder's charisma.

Discovery interviews that pitch instead of listen, ask hypothetical-intent questions ("would you buy…"), and sample only friendly contacts — manufacturing false validation at the cheapest, most dangerous stage. Prevention: interview scripts about past behavior and current spend; cold-sourced interviewees; a second team member coding transcripts independently.

Treating churn as customer success's problem when the autopsy taxonomy shows bad-fit acquisition and overpromising positioning as the top clusters. Prevention: churn-reason review includes acquisition and positioning owners; bad-fit churn is charged, organizationally, to the team that acquired it.

Either copying the incumbent's roadmap (a race the funded player wins) or claiming "we have no competitors" (the buyer always has an alternative, if only inaction). Prevention: the competitive map from market_analysis is maintained quarterly, position taken only on structural vulnerabilities, and "do nothing" always modeled as the largest competitor.

decision_gates.gate_protocol: Answer every gate yes/no with the cited evidence (metric, source, date) before committing capital to a new growth channel or major feature. A single "no" on a blocking gate stops the commitment until resolved. Thresholds may be tuned to segment and ACV in writing beforehand — never after the data arrives. Record each gate decision and its evidence; re-run the full gate set if more than one quarter passes between decision and deployment.

common_gates.gate: Is the target ICP for this investment defined, and does the evidence come from paying customers rather than prospects or pilots?
Do cohort retention curves for the affected segment flatten to a stable asymptote (rather than decline toward zero)?
Is NRR for the core ICP at or above 100%, measured over at least two quarters?
Are fully-loaded unit economics currently passing — LTV:CAC ≥ 3 computed from observed cohort retention, and CAC payback ≤ 18 months?
Is there a pre-committed success threshold, a bounded test budget, a named owner, and a kill date written down for this commitment?
Can the company absorb total loss of the committed capital without cutting runway below 12 months?
Has the assumption most likely to invalidate this investment been named, and is the test designed to expose it early rather than late?

new_channel_gates.gate: Is there direct evidence the ICP is present and reachable in this channel (not analogy from another company's playbook)?
Has a manual, low-cost probe of this channel produced at least one full-funnel conversion (first touch through activated, paying account) before scaled spend?
Is attribution instrumented end-to-end for this channel — first-touch to revenue and to cohort retention — so the readout will be causal, not anecdotal?
Does the modeled channel CAC, at fully-loaded cost and conservative conversion, keep payback inside the gate-4 threshold at the intended spend level?

Does the channel feed or build an owned compounding asset (content authority, community, list), or is it purely rented reach — and if rented, does the portfolio remain below 70% concentration after scaling it?
Will the existing team run this channel without hiring ahead of the readout (hiring waits for the test to pass)?

major_feature_gates.gate: Does the feature map to a top-ranked pain cluster from churn autopsies, activation-failure interviews, or the ICP pain list — cited by at least 5 independent ICP accounts or a top-3 churn-reason cluster?
Is the expected effect stated as a falsifiable metric movement (activation rate, NRR, win rate against a named competitor, segment churn) with a measurement plan and review date?
Has the cheapest disconfirming test been run first — problem interviews, prototype walkthroughs, a concierge/manual version, or a priced LOI — and did it pass?

Does the feature serve the retained core's workflow (deepening the moat) rather than a single deal or a hypothetical new segment — or, if it targets a new segment, has that segment independently passed gates 1–4?
Is the fully-loaded cost (build, onboarding changes, docs, support load, added surface complexity, maintenance) estimated and affordable against the expected metric movement?
Is the positioning impact written — does this feature strengthen the current axis of differentiation, and can it be attached to a named pain in outcome language on the pricing page?
Is there an explicit sunset/rollback plan if the metric movement fails to materialize by the review date, so the surface area does not accrete permanently?
